item.title: Same AI, different outcomes: what 25 lean AI startups got right
item.description: Why do lean AI startups scale while others stall? A Suvan Ventures report identifies seven growth drivers across 25 companies.
item.content:encoded:
Every AI startup today starts from the same place. The same frontier models, the same open-source alternatives, the same rented GPUs. A two-person team in Bengaluru and a thousand-person incumbent buy them on nearly the same terms.

So why do a handful of small teams scale beyond $5 million in annual recurring revenue while most stall after their first round?

That is the question behind The Lean AI Scaling Framework, a September 2026 report by Suvan Ventures Managing Partners Radhesh Kanumury and Piyush Gupta, with research intern Rahul Maran. The team studied 25 AI-native B2B companies, from Cursor and Lovable to ElevenLabs, Vapi and Legora, and catalogued 124 publicly cited reasons for their growth. Those reasons collapsed into 73 tags and, eventually, seven recurring "scaling drivers."

What is a “Lean AI Company”

For the purposes of this framework, a "Lean AI company" is defined as a company that has scaled to more than $5M in annual recurring revenue (ARR) with a core team of 10 people or more. Most companies in the 25-company sample meet this bar.

Access to AI is the baseline, not the moat

The report's starting premise is simple and direct. Since any company could ride the same AI wave, something other than AI access separates those that scale from those that don't.

What the wave did do was create opportunities. Problems that once needed a large specialist team and years of R&D became solvable by a small team on top of a purchasable or open-source building block. Natural-language coding became possible using frontier LLMs and AI coding agents, without building code-generation systems from scratch. Voice agents no longer needed proprietary speech stacks. Photorealistic video no longer needed an in-house research lab.

20 of the 25 companies (80%), formed around a specific capability wave such as RAG, agentic coding, better voice models or generative video. But the authors are careful here: timing explains why a category of startups appeared. It does not explain why one company in that category pulled ahead of rivals chasing the same opening with the same tools.

That answer sits in what founders built on top of the shared base.

The seven drivers that separated winners

Driver Seen in
(of 25)		 What it means Examples from the sample
D1 Market timing 20 Building on a capability that only just became possible Cursor, ElevenLabs, Kling AI
D2 Distribution and GTM 19 Acquiring customers without a matching sales hiring curve Lovable, Langfuse, Zapmail
D7 Problem selection 15 An acute pain tied to an existing budget and clear ROI Xbow AI, Chatbase, Legora
D4 Workflow ownership 13 Sitting inside a process the customer would have to rebuild to remove Portkey, Langfuse, Vapi
D3 Product and technical moat 10 Something a model provider cannot replicate by shipping a feature Cursor, RunwayML, Polsia AI
D6 Economics 7 Revenue that grows with usage, not headcount Bland AI, Neysa AI, Surge AI
D5 Founder-market fit 6 Founders who lived the problem at scale before building Xbow AI, Portkey, Athina AI

Three drivers do most of the explaining.

Distribution explains the "lean" part. Bottom-up developer adoption, open-source cores, freemium funnels, SEO and founder-led content let small teams grow without proportional sales hiring. Lovable is the sharpest example: the report cites roughly 8% freemium-to-paid conversion against a typical 2 to 5% SaaS benchmark, and says the company held off on a dedicated sales team until around $100M ARR. Zapmail gets about 35% of customers through affiliates.

Workflow ownership explains durability. The question the authors suggest: what would a customer have to rebuild if they stopped using you tomorrow? Gateways, observability layers and orchestration tools score highest because ripping them out means re-engineering systems and retraining teams.

Problem selection is the most controllable. It is the one driver a founder decides before writing any code. Xbow AI went after security testing, an expensive and talent-constrained bottleneck, with an ROI story framed around risk rather than productivity. Chatbase went after customer support, an existing budget line with measurable returns.

Different businesses win on different drivers

No company in the sample scored well on all seven, and the authors say none should be expected to. What matters is which drivers carry the weight for a given business model.

Archetype Sample companies Drivers that dominate
AI infrastructure and platforms Vapi, ElevenLabs, RunwayML, Neysa AI, Langfuse, Helicone, Portkey Workflow ownership (D4), technical moat (D3)
AI-native creation and development Cursor, Lovable, Emergent, Gamma, Kling AI, Legora Distribution (D2), problem selection (D7)
AI-native execution and automation Retell AI, Bland AI, Chatbase, Xbow AI, Polsia AI Problem selection (D7), economics (D6), founder-market fit (D5)
Data, training and model-ops Surge AI, Athina AI, Parea AI Workflow ownership (D4), economics via high-ACV contracts (D6)

One data point stands out in the infrastructure group. The report records three of its sample companies being acquired by larger platforms in 2026: Langfuse by ClickHouse, Helicone by Mintlify and Portkey by Palo Alto Networks. Workflow ownership, it seems, is as attractive to acquirers as it is to customers.

A scorecard founders can run on themselves

The framework ends in a practical tool. Each driver gets one diagnostic question, scored 0 (no evidence), 1 (claimed but not shown) or 2 (shown with a specific, verifiable example).

  1. Timing: What capability shift makes this possible now that wasn't possible 18 months ago?
  2. Distribution: What does it cost, in money and headcount, to win the next 50 customers?
  3. Moat: What breaks for the customer if a frontier lab ships this natively?
  4. Workflow: What would a customer have to rebuild to switch away tomorrow?
  5. Founder fit: Did you live this exact problem, at what scale, for how long?
  6. Economics: Does revenue scale with usage, or with services and support headcount?
  7. Problem: How deep it is, who pays for this today, and from which budget line

The patterns matter more than the total. A 2 on timing and little else is a company riding a wave, and its growth rate should be read as a market signal, not proof of an advantage. Strong distribution plus strong workflow ownership is the most attractive combination for capital-efficient growth. And a 0 on problem selection, a founder who cannot name the pain, the payer and the time to value, is the earliest red flag.

For Indian founders, the lesson is encouraging. Capital and compute have historically been the gap between Indian and Silicon Valley startups. If model access is now a commodity, the remaining differentiators are distribution, workflow depth and problem choice, all of which a lean Indian team can compete on. Several companies in the sample, including Portkey, Emergent and Neysa AI, were started by Indian founders.

What the framework does not claim

The authors are upfront about its limits. Every company studied had already scaled, so there is no comparison group of startups that used the same playbook and failed. The data comes from founder interviews and press coverage, where success stories tend to get simplified after the fact. One analyst did all the tagging, and 25 companies is a small, deliberately chosen sample.

So this is not a pass-or-fail scoring model, and it does not predict outcomes. It is a shared vocabulary and a set of sharper questions for the founder-investor conversation.

In a market where everyone can call the same API, "we use AI" says nothing. The questions that remain are older and harder: what pain points, who pays, how you reach them cheaply, and why they can't leave.

item.title: 5 Lessons to Learn from So Late in the Day by Claire Keegan
item.description: Discover five lessons from So Late in the Day by Claire Keegan about love, regret, gender roles, relationships, and self-awareness.
item.content:encoded:
So Late in the Day by Claire Keegan is a short but thought-provoking work of literary fiction that explores relationships, regret, gender expectations, and the quiet ways people reveal their true character.

The story follows Cathal, a man reflecting on his relationship with Sabine and the events that shaped their connection.

Through an ordinary day and memories of a relationship that did not work out, Keegan examines how everyday attitudes, small decisions, and unspoken assumptions can have lasting consequences. The story does not rely on dramatic twists to make its point.

Instead, it invites readers to look closely at the details of human behaviour and consider what they reveal about love, responsibility, and emotional maturity.

Despite its brevity, So Late in the Day raises important questions about how we treat the people closest to us and whether we recognise our own shortcomings.

5 Lessons readers can learn from Claire Keegan's book

1. Small actions reveal a person's character

One of the central lessons of So Late in the Day is that character is often revealed through ordinary behaviour rather than grand gestures.

Cathal's interactions with Sabine expose attitudes that might initially appear insignificant. His assumptions, habits, and responses to everyday situations reveal how he views relationships and the role women should play within them.

The story encourages readers to look beyond what people say about themselves. Someone may describe themselves as caring, fair, or considerate, but their everyday actions often provide a clearer picture of their values.

This lesson applies to friendships, romantic relationships, and professional environments. The way someone listens, shares responsibilities, responds to disagreement, or treats people when there is nothing to gain can tell us a great deal about their character.

Actions often communicate what words try to conceal. Paying attention to these details can help us understand others more honestly and recognise the habits we may need to change in ourselves.

2. Love requires more than good intentions

Romantic relationships cannot thrive on attraction or affection alone. They also require consideration, compromise, and a willingness to recognise another person's needs.

In So Late in the Day, Cathal's relationship with Sabine highlights the distance that can emerge when one person fails to appreciate the other fully. His perspective reveals how someone can believe they are behaving reasonably while overlooking the impact of their actions.

The story challenges the idea that being in a relationship automatically makes someone a good partner. Love involves active participation: listening, sharing responsibilities, respecting boundaries, and making space for another person's preferences.

It also requires questioning one's own assumptions rather than expecting a partner to adapt continually.

The lesson is that healthy relationships are built through everyday choices. Small acts of consideration can strengthen a connection, while repeated disregard for another person's needs can gradually undermine it.

Love is not only about what we feel for someone; it is also about how we choose to treat them.

3. Traditional gender roles can damage relationships

Claire Keegan explores how deeply traditional gender expectations can influence relationships, even when people do not openly acknowledge them.

Cathal's behaviour reflects assumptions about women, domestic responsibilities, and what a relationship should look like. These expectations shape his interactions with Sabine and reveal the imbalance that can develop when one person's comfort is prioritised over another's independence.

The story highlights how gender inequality does not always appear through obvious hostility. It can also emerge through everyday expectations, unequal responsibilities, and the belief that one partner should naturally accommodate the other.

These patterns can be difficult to recognise because they are often treated as normal. However, when they go unquestioned, they can prevent both partners from building a relationship based on genuine equality.

The lesson is to examine the expectations we bring into our relationships. Household responsibilities, emotional labour, and personal choices should not automatically fall along gender lines.

A healthy relationship allows both people to feel valued, respected, and free to make decisions about their own lives.

4. Regret often comes from what we fail to recognise

One of the most thought-provoking aspects of So Late in the Day is the way it examines regret through reflection and memory.

Cathal's recollections encourage readers to consider how people interpret their own past behaviour. We may remember certain events as insignificant while overlooking how those moments affected someone else.

Sometimes, the consequences of our choices become clearer only after a relationship has changed or an opportunity has disappeared. By then, understanding what went wrong may not be enough to repair the damage.

Keegan's story reminds us that self-awareness requires more than remembering what happened. It requires an honest examination of our own role in those events.

This lesson applies to all kinds of relationships. Instead of immediately defending our intentions, we can ask whether our behaviour was considerate and how it may have affected others.

Regret can be painful, but it can also reveal areas where we need to grow. The important thing is to learn from our mistakes while we still have the opportunity to make better choices.

Also Read
5 Books you must read to learn how to say no confidently

5. Emotional maturity begins with self-awareness

Another important lesson from the story is that emotional maturity involves recognising our own limitations and taking responsibility for our behaviour.

It is easy to believe that problems in a relationship are caused entirely by the other person. We may focus on their reactions, their expectations, or the ways they have disappointed us without examining our own contribution to the situation.

Cathal's perspective invites readers to look beyond a person's self-image and consider the gap between how someone sees themselves and how their actions affect others.

True self-awareness requires us to question our assumptions, listen to perspectives that challenge us, and acknowledge when our behaviour has been unfair.

This does not mean blaming ourselves for every problem or accepting responsibility for things beyond our control. Rather, it means recognising the parts of our behaviour that we can change.

The lesson is simple: personal growth begins when we become willing to examine ourselves honestly. Understanding our own patterns can help us build healthier relationships and avoid repeating the same mistakes.

Final thoughts

So Late in the Day by Claire Keegan explores love, gender, regret, and human behaviour through Cathal’s reflections on his relationship with Sabine. It shows how everyday actions and ingrained assumptions can shape relationships.

The five lessons highlight the importance of consideration, challenging gender expectations, learning from regret, and practising self-awareness. The story reminds us that how we treat others matters, and some lessons become clear only in hindsight.

item.title: Ather turns profitable after Rs 154 Cr loss; Meta plans to raise $35B for AI expansion
item.description: Ather Energy swung to a consolidated net profit in Q2 FY27 as revenue from operations grew 63% year-on-year. The electric two-wheeler maker plans to expand production capacity to meet rising demand.
item.content:encoded:
Dear Reader, 

MakeMyTrip is back in the black! The travel booking platform reported a net profit of $1.8 million in Q2 FY27, compared with a $5.7 million loss a year ago. Revenue rose 2.5% year-on-year to $235.2 million, or 11.2% in constant-currency terms, driven by increased bookings across categories.

Meanwhile, Anthropic, one of the leading artificial intelligence (AI) companies and the developer of the large language model Claude, has filed for an initial public offering (IPO), moving closer to becoming a publicly listed company. The company plans to list on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol ANT.

In other news, healthtech startup BioStack has raised $9.5 million in seed funding, led by Peak XV, with participation from Afore Capital, DCVC and other investors. The startup integrates fragmented clinical records to support healthcare research and clinical decision-making. It plans to use the funds to expand internationally, strengthen its technology and grow its engineering and research teams.

The AI infrastructure boom continues to gather pace. Tata Communications plans to invest $450 million to build a high-speed fibre network connecting AI data centres, catering to rising demand for AI and cloud computing infrastructure. The investment will expand its network capacity and enable faster, more reliable data transfer between data centres, which is critical for large-scale AI workloads. The move comes as technology companies ramp up investments in AI infrastructure, increasing the need for high-capacity connectivity alongside computing power. 

In a similar push to support AI expansion, Meta Platforms has launched stock and convertible preferred-stock offerings worth about $35 billion to fund its expanding AI infrastructure, including data centres and computing capacity. The Facebook and Instagram parent also plans a separate share-sale programme of up to $60 billion in 2027, potentially taking its planned equity fundraising to $95 billion.

  • Ather Energy swings to Rs 1.26 Cr profit in Q2
  • QpiAI founder makes the case for intelligence modelling

Electric Vehicle

Ather Energy swings to Rs 1.26 Cr profit in Q2

Electric two-wheeler maker Ather Energy reported a consolidated net profit of Rs 1.26 crore in Q2 FY27, compared with a net loss of Rs 154 crore in the year-ago quarter. The company’s total income rose 62% year-on-year (YoY) to Rs 1,527 crore, supported by growth in vehicle sales and operations. Ather’s performance reflects improving scale and operational efficiency as it works towards sustained profitability.

Key takeaways: 

  • Ather Energy reported a net profit of Rs 1.26 crore in Q2 FY27, compared with a loss of Rs 154 crore a year earlier. 
  • The company’s total income increased 62% YoY to Rs 1,527 crore during the quarter.
  • Vehicle volumes grew 42% YoY to 93,211 units, indicating continued demand for the company’s electric two-wheelers.

TechSparks

QpiAI founder Nagendra Nagaraja makes the case for intelligence modelling 

Nagendra Nagaraja, founder, CEO and chairman of QpiAI, believes the future of artificial intelligence lies beyond language models and conventional computing. Speaking at TechSparks 2026, he advocated for “intelligence modelling” to discover new knowledge rather than simply automate tasks. He argued that quantum computing could help overcome the limitations of silicon chips and large language models by processing complex data found in nature.

Key takeaways: 

  • Nagaraja said conventional AI relies heavily on digitised human knowledge and argued that intelligence modelling should focus on discovering what is not yet known. 
  • He highlighted quantum computing’s potential to solve complex problems in areas such as agriculture, materials science, and financial fraud detection. 
  • The Bengaluru-based company is producing 25-qubit and 64-qubit chips and building a 10-acre quantum data centre equipped with 100 quantum computers.

News & updates

  • AI Copyright: Authentic Brands Group, which owns the rights to Elvis Presley’s music and likeness, has sued AI company Anthropic for allegedly using the singer’s songs to train its models without permission. The lawsuit accuses Anthropic of infringing the rights to 274 Presley songs.
  • Oil Prices: Oil prices fell on Monday on hopes of easing US-Iran hostilities, after surging last week. However, continued attacks on Saudi Arabia kept markets on edge, with Brent crude down 1.35% to $115.15 a barrel and US WTI down 2.04% to $101.16, both near six-month highs. 

Which country has more pyramids than Egypt?

Answer: Sudan

item.title: Talent diplomacy may become the next driver of global economic growth
item.description: As ageing populations and skill shortages weigh on economies worldwide, countries are looking beyond immigration to build structured talent partnerships. India has an opportunity to emerge as a trusted global hub for workforce readiness, backed by skills training, tech and verifiable credentials.
item.content:encoded:
The drivers of economic power have always traditionally been accessing to capital, energy, technology, and markets; but more nations are now running up against that much more difficult resource to generate fast talent.

Unlike capital, talent is not something that can be conjured out of thin air overnight, it takes years to educate, train, and ready the workforce. But at the same time that world economies are in need of more workers, the number of people available is declining.

Healthcare offers one of the most transparent indicators of this situation. The World Health Organization (WHO) estimates a shortfall of 11. 1 million health and care professionals worldwide by 2030. Other sectors including manufacturing logistics hospitality, construction, and trades are experiencing similar pressures. Workforce numbers in many advanced countries are declining even as the need for core functions increases. There are declining numbers of people undertaking physically demanding jobs, leaving serious structural deficits difficult to address solely through large-scale migration.

What's left unsaid is huge: skills shortages are no longer an employment issue. They are a drag on economic growth. Countries are free to scale up investments in infrastructure, industrial capacity and technological advances, if they lack the people to run them, where is the growth?

Talent partnerships reshape economic diplomacy

Demographic decline is prompting governments to reconsider avenues for future growth. One-third of the EU population will be over 65 by the year 2050 and countries, including Japan and Germany, are already experiencing dire skill shortages within care and the healthcare sector.

Their answer has gone further than simply immigration reform. Germany's Skilled Immigration Act, Japan's increases of avenues for foreign workers and the EU's Talent Partnerships are part of a bigger change: policy makers are now starting to see "talent as a strategic asset".

These agreements are increasingly targeted on preparing the work force, recognising qualifications and moving workers, not only on visas. As countries used to compete for market access, energy, and supply chains, they are now forming partnerships to enjoy access to skilled people.

That may be one of the biggest changes to economic diplomacy in the coming decade.

India can become a global hub for workforce readiness

India’s opportunity should not be framed as the export of labour. It lies in becoming a trusted global centre for workforce readiness.

India’s domestic healthcare requirements must remain central to this approach. Responsible mobility should generate additional training capacity rather than draw indiscriminately from areas that already.

Encouragingly, this shift is already visible in policy. India plans to establish 30 Skill India International Centres focused on preparing individuals for overseas employment, while NSDC has certified over 22,455 candidates for international mobility over the past three years. The 2026 International Mobility Framework released by NITI Aayog further signals a shift in thinking, calling for greater state participation in global workforce mobility. Collectively, this suggests a larger shift where mobility of the workforce is a national asset helping create stronger economic partnerships, talent corridors, and help make India a trusted partner for the global workforce.

Technology must build trusted talent corridors

As opposed to taking over the role of educators, AI technology can assist in individualised learning, language training, workplace simulations, and competency evaluation.

Technology may minimise the information discrepancies, which have traditionally plagued international recruiting efforts. Employers require assurance that the credentials and experience are legitimate, while applicants require assurance about the legitimacy of the offer itself, along with its costs and conditions of employment.

This is increasingly becoming a competitive differentiator. ASEAN chases digital recognition of qualifications and credentials to enable smoother cross-border mobility.

For India, the opportunity is to make workforce readiness portable, verifiable and trusted. Technology can become the infrastructure that allows Indian professionals to prove their preparedness across markets, reducing friction for both employers and destination countries.

Though India's demographic weight is not the only one in an increasingly crowded field of developing countries, that invested years in creating structured talent corridors with host countries. Globally, over 8,000 nurses from Germany's Triple Win programme through government to government-built recruitment and training setups, while Japan's long standing health mobility corridors with Indonesia, the Philippines and Vietnam span language training, credentialing, and governance.

The real competition, therefore, is not for vacancies. It is for trust. Workforce shortages as a strategic challenge for ageing economies creates diplomacy where workforce readiness determines which nations become indispensable partners in supporting global growth.

(Mayank Kumar is the Co-founder & CEO of BorderPlus)

item.title: Build, scale, and govern AI agents: Inside Google Cloud’s Gemini roadmap
item.description: Join Google Cloud product leaders for the latest on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and Gemini Enterprise for Customer Experience.
item.content:encoded:
Lean teams rarely lack ambition. What they lack is the headcount to turn it into production-ready AI, from the engineers who build agents to the security staff who keep them in check.

That is the gap Google Cloud’s next webinar, in partnership with YourStory, is built to address. On October 30, Google Cloud product leaders will present ‘The Gemini roadmap’, a briefing on the latest GeminiAI updates, including the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform and Gemini Enterprise for Customer Experience.

Tailored for lean organizations, the session looks at how AI can act as a true force multiplier for a team. Drawing on the 2026 Gemini roadmap, attendees will gain the proven ROI frameworks and technical deep-dives needed to stay agile and competitive in a rapidly evolving market.

The briefing is split into two sessions, each built for a different audience.

Build, scale, and govern agents with the Agent Platform

The first session is best suited to technical leaders and developers. It will explore the latest features of the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, which combines Google’s leading AI research with secure, global infrastructure so teams can build, scale, and manage agents that actually work in production. The idea is a secure, all-in-one platform for the entire agent lifecycle, a digital ‘extra set of hands’ that handles complex workflows reliably.

Attendees will get to see how to build quickly with the Agent Development Kit (ADK), launch agents into production through a fully managed, integrated runtime, and use Agent Gateway and Agent Identity to manage permissions and security without a massive security team. The session will also cover automatically applying and enforcing security policies as deployments grow, and making agents accessible to every employee through the Gemini app.

Three Google Cloud product leaders will present this session: Jamie de Guerre, Senior Director, Product Management, Cloud AI; Shubham Saboo, Senior AI Product Manager; and Dmitry Pimenov, Director, Product Management, Gemini 

Unify the customer journey with Gemini for customer experience

The second session is aimed at business leaders focused on customer experience. It will start from a familiar frustration: disconnected apps and missed customer opportunities, when every interaction counts, from the first inquiry to the final checkout. Attendees will witness how to build AI agents that handle the heavy lifting and provide natural, helpful support across the entire customer journey.

This segment is for leaders ready to move past basic chatbots. It will show how the same technology used by global brands to double their efficiency can be put to work for a growing team. Gemini 3.1 Live Audio gives a brand a natural voice that resolves issues through fluid conversation rather than rigid menus. A smart context engine remembers what the customer said three steps ago, so they never have to repeat themselves. Automated insights identify customer trends instantly, helping teams improve service with every call, while enterprise-grade privacy keeps business and customer data under their exclusive control.

This session will be led by Ali Rana, Director of Product for Applied AI at Google Cloud, who will conduct the Customer Experience session.

Why this matters

For lean organizations, the next stage of AI adoption is less about experimentation and more about execution: shipping agents that hold up in production, keeping them secure, and delivering customer support that feels natural rather than scripted. A massive engineering or security department is not something every lean team has.

This webinar is designed to show that it does not have to be a prerequisite. By pairing a technical view of the Agent Platform with a business view of customer experience, it gives both builders and decision-makers a clear picture of what is coming and how to put it to work.

Register now to secure your spot and get ready for what’s next with Gemini

item.title: Soulflower's Natasha Tuli on why brands must earn customer trust
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Soulflower Founder Natasha Tuli explained why advertising and discounts may attract customers, but transparency, product quality, and listening to consumers are what bring them back.
item.content:encoded:
Advertising and discounts can attract customers, but getting them to return takes more than marketing.

At TechSparks 2026 in Bengaluru, Natasha Tuli, Founder, CEO and Chief Formulator of Soulflower, spoke about the importance of building customer trust during a session titled ‘Everyone can build a brand. How many can build a belief?’

Tuli discussed how Soulflower has used product innovation, transparency, and direct conversations with customers to build loyalty.

Attention is the easy part

Meta ads and discounts can help brands attract attention, Tuli said, but a first purchase only shows that the marketing has worked. A repeat purchase indicates that the product has delivered on its promise.

She also spoke about the tendency of brands to copy one another rather than develop products that stand out.

“You can come up with something really innovative and different… and you can stick with it. People will soon believe in it,” she said.

Citing Google Trends data, Tuli said searches for rosemary rose nearly sevenfold between 2021 and 2026. Interest in rosemary oil increased after the COVID-19 pandemic, she said, when Soulflower began selling larger quantities and educating customers about how to use it.

Soap was another example. At a time when shower gels were popular, Tuli chose to make oil-based soap priced at Rs 400.

She recalled a meeting with Wipro, where she was asked how Soulflower could sell sandalwood soap at that price when Wipro’s product was considerably cheaper.

Instead of simply defending the price, Tuli decided to show customers how the soap was made. She began filming the production process despite warnings that she was revealing trade secrets.

“Everybody in India making their own soap? It’s not going to happen,” she said. “I don’t think anybody started a soap business after this, but I definitely increased a lot of my sales.”

For Tuli, showing customers how products are made helps build confidence in the brand.

“Customers enjoy knowing how you are making this thing, or who the people behind it are. It gives them a sneak peek inside the soul of your brand, which is so important,” she said.

Choose the customer first

Tuli said Soulflower photographs customers' shopping carts to understand what else they buy alongside its products. She studies these purchases to learn more about their preferences.

“Everything sells,” she said. “You can sell anything. The question is, to whom do you want to sell, and at what price, and what is the promise that you’re going to give to that customer.” This approach led Soulflower to develop a non-oily rosemary hair serum.

Tuli said many customers in North India disliked applying oil to their hair. However, her co-founder was initially reluctant to introduce the serum because oils had long been central to the brand. It took her two years to convince him.

“I was thinking not of myself. I was thinking of my customer,” she said.

Staying accessible to customers

Tuli also spoke about the importance of being available to customers and responding to their questions.

She said she personally holds the passwords to Soulflower's social media accounts and often responds to customer messages late at night, after midnight, when other team members are unavailable.

“If anybody messages or DMs me, there will be an answer,” she said, adding that customers often do not realise they are speaking directly to her.

However, she acknowledged that responding personally to every message is not sustainable as the business grows.

“Is Natasha going to be answering all these people every night? No, I can’t do it,” she said.

To address this, Tuli developed ‘Ask Natasha’, a bot built using technology and her past conversations with customers. The bot responds to late-night messages in the way she would, allowing the brand to continue answering questions when she is unavailable.

Tuli ended the session by asking founders to consider three questions: why customers choose their brand, why they return, and how the brand can retain their trust as it grows.

She also invited founders to reach out to her, but asked them not to pitch their products.

“Go talk to your customer,” she said. “Don’t talk at them. Talk to them and listen to them.”

Edited by Teja Lele

item.title: Collective Artists Network’s Vijay Subramaniam on AI and the changing media landscape
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Collective Artists Network founder Vijay Subramaniam discussed how AI is reshaping content creation, democratising storytelling, and changing the economics of entertainment.
item.content:encoded:
For years, the media industry has operated in silos. Talent agencies managed stars, studios made films, platforms distributed content, and brands paid to reach audiences.

Today, those boundaries are blurring. Creators are building their own businesses, AI is changing how content is made, and a single story or character can become the starting point for films, series, brand partnerships, and more.

The Collective Artists Network, founded by Vijay Subramaniam, is building across many of these areas.

In a fireside chat titled The great media rebundle: Why content, talent, technology and commerce are coming together at TechSparks 2026, Subramaniam discussed how his venture is building layers across talent communities, marketing communities, and technology, and how AI fits into the larger scheme.

Dubbed the “AI man of the media industry”, Subramaniam said that, though it’s scary, he wears the badge with confidence because technology is here to stay.

“My fundamental belief is that content creation should be a level playing field. Historically, a few elites have always had the opportunity to tell a story. But anyone with a story should be able to tell and consume it. My company is pursuing that aggressively. We have the largest slate of AI-enabled content in the world today, and we’re very excited about it,” he explained.

As the media business changes, what does it stand to gain and what does it stand to lose?

Subramaniam believes the media business is recession-proof. 

“When COVID happened, we were all confined to our houses to consume content. I don’t think the media stands to lose anything. The operators of media stand to lose if they don’t move with the times.”

He pointed out that for the first time, the Indian media ecosystem is seeing the death of oligarchs.

“Look at everything that has done well, from the pandemic years onward: KGF, Mahavatar Narsimha, the shows on Netflix. We just produced a beautiful little show called Musafir Cafe, which blew up on Netflix. Look at Aditya Dhar and Ranveer [Singh] and what they did with Dhurandhar. These are not people who have been around for 40 to 50 years gatekeeping the industry. These are new names, fresh faces, fresh talent that has broken through. I think that’s what will succeed,” he said.

But is AI making content cheaper? Will it make businesses more profitable and allow them to make content at a fraction of the earlier cost?

“Will businesses be more profitable because of it? Two hundred per cent, yes. Will storytelling now be democratic, so that you can sit in Jabalpur or Coimbatore and tell a story? Yes. What we’re bringing to the table is this: if you have a vision, you can realise it,” he said.

Subramaniam also emphasised that it’s not typing a prompt and getting a script, or “AI slop”. 

"The same principles that apply in animation apply here. You need a production designer, a costume designer, a DOP. There will never be a point where AI cracks the script and the dialogue." 

“You’ll need a human behind it. Nobody can capture a director’s vision. We’ve built our [G5] tool entirely on the back of working with four National Award-winning directors: Rajesh [Mapuskar], who won for Ventilator; Hansal Mehta; Sanjay Puran Singh [Chauhan]; and Manu Anand. They told us what they needed built into the product, and that’s what you see us building today,” he added.

Speaking about Mahabharat, a fully AI-generated animated and visual series released late 2025, Subramaniam admitted to learnings from the first release.

“Did we learn a lot from that first release? Yes. Are we proud of it? Yes, because we’re the first in the world to do it. More importantly, we’ve built the tech so well that in our subsequent releases, starting next month, you’ll see the enhancement. Today we actually have emotion. We have comic timing. We have genuine stress, grief and other expressions coming alive through the tools,” he said.

The creator economy is evolving rapidly, with artificial intelligence, new business models and direct-to-consumer brands opening up opportunities for creators to build businesses. But as the industry looks to the next five years, the bigger question is what will drive success: talent, stories or access to audiences?

For Vijay Subramaniam, the answer begins with recognising that audiences are becoming increasingly difficult to predict.

“The audience is tougher than it has ever been. Every time you say, ‘This is a formula’, it breaks,” he said, pointing to how audience preferences can defy even the most established industry assumptions.

A title like Musafir Cafe challenges the belief that big-budget streaming shows need the scale and spectacle of Game of Thrones or House of the Dragon. Similarly, the belief that audiences won't commit time to theatrical releases can be upended by the success of films like Dhurandhar.

In an environment where established formulas offer little certainty, Subramaniam believes the fundamentals of building a successful creative business remain unchanged: find the right storytellers, equip them with the resources they need, and ensure the economics make sense.

“What you need to keep in view is: one, catch the best storyteller with the most passion. Two, give them everything they need from a tools standpoint. Three, don’t be stupid about economics,” he said.

item.title: 5 Lessons to Learn from Why Does He Do That? by Lundy Bancroft
item.description: Discover five powerful lessons from Lundy Bancroft’s Why Does He Do That? about abusive behaviour, emotional manipulation, power, and healthy relationships.
item.content:encoded:
Why does someone who claims to love you also make you feel afraid, guilty, or unworthy? In Why Does He Do That? Inside the Minds of Angry and Controlling Men, author Lundy Bancroft explores the behaviour of abusive and controlling men, challenging common misconceptions about abuse and relationships.

Drawing on his experience working with abusive men, Bancroft explains how controlling behaviour can develop through beliefs about entitlement, power, and relationships. The book encourages readers to look beyond apologies and promises and pay attention to patterns of behaviour.

5 Important lessons to learn from the book

1. Abuse is about power and control

One of the central lessons of the book is that abuse is not always about anger or losing control. It can also involve deliberate attempts to maintain power over a partner.

Abusive behaviour may include monitoring someone's activities, restricting their friendships, controlling finances, or making them feel guilty for expressing their needs. These actions can gradually undermine a person's independence.

Bancroft encourages readers to recognise that abuse involves more than physical violence. Emotional manipulation, intimidation, and coercive control can also cause significant harm.

Lesson: A healthy relationship respects your independence. Love should never require you to surrender your freedom, friendships, or sense of self.

2. Apologies do not always mean change

An apology can feel reassuring, especially when someone you love promises never to hurt you again. However, Bancroft highlights the importance of examining what happens after the apology.

In unhealthy relationships, apologies may be followed by affection, promises, and temporary improvements. Yet the same harmful behaviour can return when the person feels comfortable again.

Genuine change requires more than regret. It involves accepting responsibility, acknowledging the harm caused, challenging harmful beliefs, and consistently behaving differently over time.

It is also important to remember that not every apology is manipulative. The key is whether the person takes meaningful responsibility and respects the other person's boundaries.

Lesson: Do not judge change by promises alone. Look for consistent actions, accountability, and respect over time.

3. You are not responsible for someone else's abusive behaviour

People experiencing abuse often question themselves. They may wonder whether they were too demanding, too emotional, or not understanding enough. They might even believe that behaving differently could prevent future incidents.

Bancroft challenges this way of thinking by examining the attitudes and beliefs that can underpin abusive behaviour. A person's decision to intimidate, manipulate, or control their partner is not simply the result of their partner's imperfections.

Every relationship has disagreements, and both people can make mistakes. However, ordinary conflict is different from a repeated pattern of intimidation, humiliation, or control.

Understanding this distinction can help people stop carrying responsibility for behaviour they did not choose.

Lesson: You can reflect on your own actions without accepting blame for another person's decision to abuse or control you.

4. Emotional manipulation can be difficult to recognise

Abuse does not always begin with obvious threats or aggression. Sometimes, it develops through subtle behaviours that gradually affect a person's confidence and understanding of their own experiences.

A controlling partner might dismiss your feelings, blame you for every disagreement, question your memory, or make you feel selfish for setting boundaries. Over time, these patterns can leave you doubting your judgement and prioritising the other person's emotions over your own wellbeing.

Bancroft's work encourages readers to examine the broader pattern rather than treating every incident as an isolated disagreement.

Also Read
Beat manipulation: 5 mind games and how to outsmart them

Not every argument or insensitive comment is evidence of abuse. What matters is the repeated use of behaviour to intimidate, diminish, or control another person.

Lesson: Pay attention to patterns that make you feel afraid, powerless, or constantly responsible for keeping someone else happy. Your feelings and boundaries deserve respect.

5. You cannot change someone who refuses to take responsibility

One of the most difficult lessons in the book is that love, patience, and understanding cannot guarantee that an abusive person will change.

A partner may have experienced trauma, struggled with anger, or faced difficult circumstances. These experiences can help explain aspects of someone's behaviour, but they do not excuse abuse.

Lasting change requires the person engaging in harmful behaviour to recognise the problem, challenge their sense of entitlement, accept responsibility, and make sustained efforts to behave differently.

The person experiencing abuse cannot do this work on their behalf. They are not obligated to remain in a harmful relationship while waiting for change.

If you are experiencing abuse, seeking support from trusted people or a domestic abuse service can help you understand your options and consider your safety.

Lesson: You can care about someone without taking responsibility for fixing them. Protecting your wellbeing is not a failure of love.

Final thoughts

Why Does He Do That? by Lundy Bancroft offers a deeper understanding of abusive and controlling behaviour, helping readers recognise patterns that can otherwise be difficult to explain.

Its central message is that abuse should not be dismissed as ordinary relationship conflict, uncontrolled anger, or a problem that one partner can solve through greater patience. Understanding the role of power, entitlement, and accountability can help people evaluate their relationships more clearly.

Ultimately, a healthy relationship should make room for mutual respect, personal freedom, emotional safety, and accountability. Love is not measured by how much mistreatment someone can tolerate, but by how both people treat each other.

item.title: Anthropic files for IPO even as losses surge to $80B
item.description: Anthropic will be listed on the Nasdaq stock exchange and will trade under the name of ANT.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic, one of the leading artificial intelligence (AI) companies and the developer of the large language model Claude, has filed for an initial public offering (IPO), moving closer to becoming a publicly listed company.

The company plans to list on the Nasdaq stock exchange under the ticker symbol ANT.

Anthropic was co-founded by Dario Amodei and others in 2021. In the first half of 2026, it reported revenue of $16.2 billion, while losses stood at $80.74 billion. In comparison, the company reported revenue of $1.16 billion and losses of $12.96 billion in the first half of 2025.

Anthropic’s growth has been remarkable, with revenue rising from just $41 million in 2023 to $4.5 billion in 2025.

However, the company has not specified a date for its Nasdaq listing, disclosed the proposed share price or stated how much it plans to raise through the IPO.

Anthropic’s IPO is expected to be closely watched across the technology industry, given the rapid advances made by AI companies. The company was valued at $965 billion in its most recent funding round in May 2026.

Interestingly, Anthropic market rival OpenAI has said it will go for a public listing next year.

In its IPO filing, Anthropic said, “We believe that AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history. If managed well, it could rapidly accelerate scientific innovation, greatly increase economic growth rates, bring cures for major diseases within reach and solve problems that have resisted generations of human efforts.”

“Anthropic aims to realise these while navigating and preventing the risks that come with a technological revolution this fast and this powerful.”

Anthropic believes the diffusion of AI through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and it is just beginning. It further noted that the world has only begun to use the capabilities of today’s frontier models, and the gap between what Claude can do and how broadly it is used represents one of our largest growth opportunities, alongside continued advances at the frontier.

item.title: Told to give up science in school, Mallikarjuna Iytha now backs 2,000 entrepreneurs with disabilities
item.description: Mallikarjuna Iytha, told to drop science due to disability, founded IDEA to back 2,000+ entrepreneurs with disabilities in India.
item.content:encoded:
Living with 88% locomotor disability, the National Award-winning founder of IDEA has spent seven years making one argument: persons with disabilities should be treated as entrepreneurs and job creators, not welfare recipients.

Mallikarjuna Iytha was in Class XI when he was told to drop science.

The reason was not his marks. It was his disability. Science, he was advised, would be too hard for someone with 88% locomotor disability. The arts would be more practical.

That advice would follow him in different forms for years. Today, it is the reason he runs the Inclusive Divyangjan Entrepreneur Association (IDEA), an organisation that says it has supported more than 2,000 entrepreneurs with disabilities across India.

His work since has been built on refusing to let anyone else decide how far a person with a disability can go.

Three closed doors

The first door was science in school. The second came years later, when Iytha set out to pursue doctoral research in environmental science and met the same doubts about whether someone with his disability could do the work.

The third was quieter. In the corporate sector, he found that getting hired was not the same as being considered for leadership. Persons with disabilities could be employed. They were rarely expected to lead.

Together, those experiences pushed him towards one question: what would change if persons with disabilities were seen not as beneficiaries, but as entrepreneurs, leaders and creators of economic value?

An alumnus of Jawaharlal Nehru University, Iytha built a long career in India's development sector. He went on to serve as president of Fair Trade Forum-India, the national network that represents the World Fair Trade Organization in India and works with grassroots artisans and farmers.

In 2017, when Delhi hosted World Fair Trade Week and the 14th WFTO Biennial Conference, the forum was among the organisers and Iytha was its president. Linking marginalised producers to markets, rather than to aid alone, would become central to what he built next.

From question to IDEA

Iytha spent years studying the aspirations, barriers and economic realities of persons with disabilities before founding IDEA in 2019.

The organisation was built to work across the full journey, from an entrepreneur's first idea to running and growing a business. Its support combines entrepreneurship training, mentoring, employment, financial help, accessibility and market access.

The premise is a deliberate break from welfare. Instead of asking what persons with disabilities need to receive, IDEA asks what they need in order to build.

The numbers have grown steadily. When Iytha received his national award in December 2024, IDEA was recognised for supporting more than 1,060 entrepreneurs with disabilities. By March 2025, the New Delhi-based not-for-profit said it had backed over 1,500 entrepreneurs across 11 states, whose businesses had together generated about Rs 100 crore in turnover. IDEA now puts the count at more than 2,000.

The organisation has also helped persons with disabilities into jobs. In May 2025, it said more than 5,000 people had found employment through its work.

One of those entrepreneurs is Sonia. She was diagnosed with muscular dystrophy while studying for her BCom, which left her with 75% disability. Struggling with depression and isolation, she had nearly given up on her plans until she connected with IDEA. She now leads her own self-help group and runs an enterprise that employs other women.

Money that keeps moving

One of Iytha's signature ideas is the Divyangjan Hunar Atmanirbhar Network, or DHAN.

It works like a revolving fund. Entrepreneurs receive seed support to get started. Once their businesses succeed, they contribute back to a common pool, which then funds the next person. Support does not end with one beneficiary; it keeps circulating.

For Iytha, the design is the philosophy. Empowerment lasts when people can create value, make their own choices and give back to the system that helped them.

DHAN has become IDEA's flagship programme. By March 2025, it had supported more than 1,200 entrepreneurs with disabilities across 10 states through training, mentoring, financial aid and market access.

That month, many of them showed their products at the Ability Expo organised by IDEA at Purple Fest 2025 in New Delhi, which President Droupadi Murmu opened.

The model is also spreading through partnerships. With the Andhra Pradesh MedTech Zone (AMTZ) in Visakhapatnam, IDEA runs a programme that offers entrepreneurship training, seed funding, market linkages and two years of handholding. AMTZ also buys products made by the entrepreneurs it supports. The aim, Iytha said, is to help Divyangjan become "active contributors to society and the economy."

Beyond business

Iytha argues that a loan and a business plan are not enough. An entrepreneur with a disability also needs accessible transport, workplaces, buildings, digital systems and markets.

That thinking produced Sugamya Delhi Abhiyaan. It grew out of a campaign in Dwarka, launched on 1 May 2025, in which more than 500 experts and volunteers audited over 70 buildings and public spaces for accessibility in just 15 days. They covered government offices, schools, colleges, banks, bus stops, parks and footpaths.

The citywide campaign was launched on 17 May 2025, Global Accessibility Awareness Day, at the office of the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities. More than 100 stakeholders pledged support. "Accessibility must now become a people's movement, not just a government initiative," Iytha said at the launch.

Two tools came out of the event: a Purple Building Certification Scheme for accessible buildings, developed jointly by IDEA, AMTZ and ICMR, and IDEA's own accessibility guidelines for events.

He has also brought a researcher's lens to the problem, co-authoring academic work on entrepreneurship among persons with disabilities, including how uncertainty and technology shape their journeys.

Recognition, and what it stands for

On 3 December 2024, International Day of Persons with Disabilities, President Droupadi Murmu presented Iytha with the National Award for Individual Excellence in the Sarvshresth Divyangjan category. The citation recognised his work on empowering persons with disabilities, inclusive growth, disability rights and social entrepreneurship.

The honour matters beyond him. It acknowledges the argument he has been making for years: that disability inclusion has to mean opportunity, enterprise and economic participation, not just access to schemes.

Believing is seeing

Iytha sums up his approach in three words: "Believing is Seeing." Opportunity, he says, begins when society believes in what a person can do.

His larger goal is an India where persons with disabilities do not just fit into existing systems, but build businesses, create jobs, lead institutions and shape policy themselves.

The targets ahead are bigger still. By 2027, IDEA aims to train 5,000 entrepreneurs with disabilities, create 10,000 jobs and help their businesses reach a combined Rs 1,500 crore in turnover.

He started out being told to settle for a smaller dream. He has spent his career making room for bigger ones.

item.title: Matiks raises $10M in pre-Series A round led by General Catalyst
item.description: The company said it will use the funding to expand internationally, develop new games and social experiences, and launch an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered game creation platform that will enable users to build and publish games without writing code.
item.content:encoded:
Bengaluru-based social gaming platform Matiks has raised $10 million in a pre-Series A funding round led by General Catalyst. The round also saw participation from entrepreneur Ronnie Screwvala and existing investors Info Edge Ventures, Tanglin Venture Partners, and Untitled Ventures.

According to a statement by the company, the fresh capital will be used to expand internationally, develop new games and social experiences, and launch an artificial intelligence (AI)-powered game creation platform that will enable users to build and publish games without writing code.

Founded in 2024, Matiks develops games centred on mathematics, memory, logic and puzzles, combining competitive gameplay with social features.

In September 2026, 2.2 million people played 48 million games on the platform. Its daily active users have more than doubled since June to over 300,000, with early engagement emerging in markets including Japan, the US and South Korea, the compamy said.

“Over the last decade, we have made it incredibly easy to consume content but have done far less to make using our brains equally entertaining. We started Matiks with a simple belief: using your brain can be just as fun and addictive as any other form of entertainment," said Sudhanshu Bhatia, co-founder and chief executive officer of Matiks.

"Our ambition is to make mind sports as culturally relevant as physical sports and esports - giving mental athletes, puzzlers, and competitive players the visibility, communities, and recognition they deserve. With AI, we want anyone, anywhere in the world, to create a brain game that millions can play. We are not trying to get people off their phones; we are trying to give them something better to do on them,” he added.

The company said users who complete a seven-day streak show 62% retention one month later, while some early cohorts have retained 32% of users at week 52. Its recently launched single-player puzzle format, SNAC, has also driven longer engagement, with sessions that include the format running approximately three times longer.

Rahul Humayan, partner at General Catalyst, said the platform was addressing demand for alternatives to conventional digital content.

"Negative content is consuming a growing share of our screen time, and Matiks is building the alternative: a social platform for brain games where people challenge friends, learn from one another and, soon, use AI to create games of their own. Sudhanshu, Sushant and Mohan have built one of the most engaged communities we have seen in consumer, from everyday players to world champions, and they are now taking it global. We are proud to partner with them as they make brain games a category of their own," he said.

Matiks will initially prioritise expansion in the US before entering other tier-one markets. It also plans to increase investments in engineering, AI, product, design, game development and growth, alongside scaling creator partnerships and global distribution.

The company plans to develop an AI-powered game creation engine that will allow users to create, publish and share brain games across multiple formats. It expects user-generated content to increase the variety of games available on the platform.

item.title: Tata Comm to invest $450M in high-speed fibre network to connect AI data centres
item.description: The first phase of the programme will focus on the Mumbai-Pune-Hyderabad-Chennai corridor, one of India's most important Al and hyperscale growth routes.
item.content:encoded:
Tata Communications on Monday said it plans to invest $450 million (about Rs 4,280 crore) for setting up a high-speed long-haul fibre network in India to connect AI data centres.

The first phase of the programme will focus on the Mumbai-Pune-Hyderabad-Chennai corridor, one of India's most important Al and hyperscale growth routes.

Subsequent phases will expand connectivity into emerging East Coast and Western India data centre ecosystems, including Vizag, Bhubaneswar, Jamnagar, GIFT City and other strategic locations, the company said in a statement.

"Tata Communications...announced strategic investments of close to USD 450 million to build an Al super highway in India - a high-speed, low-latency network fabric connecting India's key Al data-centre corridors. The company will build around 10,000 kilometers of the new long-haul fibre across India, creating one of the country's largest Al-ready connectivity networks," it said.

Integrated with Tata Communications' global network backbone, the Al network aims to provide customers with a seamless, end-to-end connectivity fabric, supporting the performance, resilience and scale required for next-generation Al workloads.

"We are excited about the opportunity in the India data centre-to-data centre connectivity, which we believe could evolve into a market exceeding USD 1 billion over the medium term. With our planned investments, we are building on our existing strengths to create one of the most comprehensive data centre connectivity platforms in the market. As we scale, a growing proportion of our expansion is being driven by anchor customer commitments and contracted demand," MD and CEO Ganesh Lakshminarayanan said.

Tata Communications said it will enable seamless connectivity between India and major global Al hubs across, positioning India as a strategic gateway in the global digital infrastructure landscape.

In parallel, the company will continue to cater to the requirement of existing enterprise and data centre connectivity requirements by scaling its current national long distance and metro network footprint.

Tata Communications operates one of the largest wholly-owned subsea fibre networks spanning over 5 lakh kilometer of subsea optical fibre and over 2 lakh km of terrestrial fibre.

The company said it enhanced Tata Global Network (TGN) capabilities in June 2026 by planning a new subsea cable system between Mumbai and Singapore and invested as a consortium member in a new subsea cable system, connecting Chennai to Singapore, which is expected to be ready for service in the last quarter of 2029.

item.title: India's voice AI challenges could shape global technology, says Murf AI co-founder
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Sneha Roy, the co-founder and COO of Murf AI, explains how multilingual speech, smaller AI models, and cost-efficient infrastructure can make voice agents work across markets.
item.content:encoded:
What Indian users consider an ordinary conversation could be the toughest test for voice AI, and solving it could unlock applications worldwide.

An AI voice can answer a question, confirm an order or help book a reservation. But can it pronounce an Indian name correctly, understand an address spoken in a mix of Hindi and English, and respond quickly enough to sound natural?

For Sneha Roy, the co-founder and COO of Murf AI, these are not exceptional scenarios. They are the baseline for building voice AI that works for India and, ultimately, the world.

During a masterclass on ‘Building voice AI from India, for India, and for the world’, at TechSparks 2026, Roy explained how India’s linguistic complexity, infrastructure constraints, and cost considerations are influencing the development of speech technology.

When edge cases become the specification

Roy drew parallels with products that adapted to Indian users before finding wider applications. Google Maps introduced offline functionality for areas with limited internet connectivity, while Netflix introduced a mobile-only plan that, Roy said, has since been adopted in 78 countries. Uber piloted cash rides in Hyderabad, before expanding the option to other markets.

She believes voice AI could follow a similar path.

Consider a routine delivery-status call in Bengaluru. A customer might combine English with a regional language, use a locally familiar pronunciation of an address, and expect a PIN code to be spoken digit by digit. A model built around standardised English can struggle with these details.

“If the customer has to change something about the way they speak just to get the agent to cope up, or keep repeating their address or their name, we haven’t finished building it yet,” said Roy.

For her, the challenge is to build systems that accommodate how people naturally speak, rather than expecting customers to adapt to the technology.

Smaller models, faster conversations

Natural speech is only one part of the problem. Voice agents must also respond quickly and operate economically at scale, where businesses may handle millions of calls each month.

Roy said the complete voice-agent pipeline, including speech recognition, the language model and speech generation, typically has a response budget of 500–800 milliseconds. Murf has worked to bring its text-to-speech model latency below 100 milliseconds, including network delays, she said.

To achieve this, the company developed Falcon 2, a smaller speech model designed to run across a wider range of GPUs rather than depend on specific, high-end hardware. Roy said this approach has helped maintain low latency across different geographies while improving cost efficiency.

The same engineering choices can benefit markets beyond India, particularly where computing infrastructure is limited or deploying voice agents at scale remains expensive.

Building trust alongside natural speech

Roy also highlighted the importance of responsible voice data practices. Murf works with more than 400 voice actors globally through long-term, royalty-based partnerships, she said, and does not clone voices without consent.

For customers with strict privacy requirements, the company offers APIs that can process data without retaining it, as well as on-premises deployments for sensitive applications.

Roy’s central argument is that India’s linguistic diversity and infrastructure constraints should not be treated as secondary requirements. They can help define what voice AI needs to do before it is ready for widespread adoption.

As she put it, “India is the spec capital of the world.”

item.title: MakeMyTrip rebounds in Q2 FY27 with $1.8M profit
item.description: The company noted that its agentic platform Myra engaged in over 90,000 daily conversations across multiple Indian languages and English, of which more than 55% originated from Tier II and Tier III cities in the second quarter of FY27.
item.content:encoded:
Digital travel booking platform MakeMyTrip swung back into profit for the three months ending September, 2026 boosted by increased booking across all categories.

The company reported a net profit of $1.8 million for the second quarter of FY27 as compared to loss of $5.7 million in the similar period a year ago. The revenue for the second quarter touched $235.2 million which was a 11.2% increase when compared to the similar period of last fiscal.

On the performance of the company, MakeMyTrip Group Chief Executive Officer Rajesh Magow said, “We delivered strong growth despite a challenging travel environment, with Gross Bookings increasing 20.9% year on year in constant currency to $2.7 billion. Growth in hotels and ground transport underscored the resilience of our diversified portfolio and our ability to serve evolving customer needs.”

A statement from MakeMyTrip noted that the annual growth in adjusted margin in the air ticketing business was 14.3%, hotels and packages (20.2%), bus ticketing (29%)n and Others growing 29.8%.

The company noted that its agentic platform Myra engaged in over 90,000 daily conversations across multiple Indian languages and English, of which more than 55% originated from Tier II and Tier III cities in the second quarter of FY27.

It further added that Myra resolved over 53% of post-booking queries in relation to flights and hotels and emphasised that this platform has capabilities spanning end-to-end trip planning, voice interactions and in-chat payments and assisted on an average of more than 3,000 completed bookings per.day.

MakeMyTrip highlighted that its customers engaging with Myra completed approximately 1.7 times more bookings compared with non-Myra users. In addition, customers from Tier II and Tier III cities in India engaging with Myra completed approximately 2.1 times more bookings compared with non-Myra users for the second quarter.

“We are using AI to simplify travel planning and booking, supported by our extensive supply network, integrated distribution platform and trusted service. We continue to invest with discipline to capture India’s long-term travel opportunity and deliver sustainable, profitable growth,” Magow said.

item.title: How Attero is using AI to solve recycling’s pricing and compliance challenges
item.description: At TechSparks 2026, Ayush Agarwal, Head of Product and Technology at Attero, explains how AI-powered systems are helping the e-waste recycler standardise scrap pricing, automate compliance and improve financial visibility.
item.content:encoded:
A washing machine arriving at a recycling plant may look like a single product.

For a recycler, however, its value depends on what is inside, which components are missing, how much material can be recovered, and what it will cost to process.

Multiply those decisions across thousands of appliances, suppliers and locations, and recycling becomes a complex exercise in pricing, logistics and compliance.

At Attero, an Indian e-waste and battery recycling company, artificial intelligence is helping bring these decisions into a common system.

Speaking at TechSparks 2026, Ayush Agarwal, Head of Product and Technology at Attero, outlined how the company is using AI to value recyclable materials and ensure transactions comply with regulatory requirements.

Pricing scrap beyond human judgement

Attero processes around 200,000 metric tonnes of e-waste and 10,000 metric tonnes of lithium-ion batteries annually, Agarwal said. The company procures material worth more than Rs 1,000 crore a year, making accurate pricing important to its economics.

Unlike copper or gold, scrap does not have a single standard price on global commodity exchanges. Its value depends on recoverable materials, processing and transportation costs, as well as regional demand and supply.

Attero has built Matrix, an AI-powered pricing engine combining material intelligence with market intelligence. It estimates the components and recoverable metals in different appliances, and then uses machine learning models and commodity prices to calculate what the material should cost in a particular market.

A washing machine, for instance, could command different prices in Delhi and Mumbai because of logistics costs and local market conditions. The system draws on three years of recycling data, two years of exchange data, and information covering thousands of appliances.

“These decisions do not scale with human judgement,” Agarwal said, explaining why the company wanted to standardise pricing rather than expand teams to manage growing volumes.

Turning compliance into a data system

Pricing is only one challenge. Recycling companies must also maintain extensive records covering suppliers, transporters, invoices, vehicle documents, and regulatory requirements.

Attero has also developed Lightspeed, an AI-powered compliance engine that checks documents, reconciles information across records and flags exceptions for review. The system is designed to produce audit-ready reports that can help the company respond to regulatory or client queries years after a transaction.

Attero’s platform has processed 50,000 documents and flagged over 500 errors so far, according to Agarwal. The company aims to improve efficiency by 70%, enabling its existing team to handle four times as many documents without increasing headcount.

Making business performance visible

For Agarwal, AI’s value extends beyond automation. Connecting pricing decisions, procurement costs and recovered material values gives Attero a clearer view of profitability at the individual order level.

He said the company is also developing visual learning capabilities to identify incoming material from supplier images, with its image dataset growing from 10,000 towards a target of 100,000.

The broader lesson is that AI can create business value even in industries where the work remains physical. By making decisions more consistent and bringing fragmented operational data together, Attero strives to build systems designed to support growth without relying entirely on more people.

item.title: Healthtech startup BioStack raises $9.5M in seed funding round led by Peak XV, others
item.description: BioStack creates workflows that bring together clinical information across disparate health systems and geographies. It currently works with hospitals across the US, Brazil, India and Argentina.
item.content:encoded:
Healthcare technology company BioStack has raised $9.5 million in a seed funding round led by Peak XV, Afore Capital, DCVC, Emerson Collective, SV Angel, Verdict Capital, Streamlined Ventures, and Y Combinator. 

The round will support BioStack's continued expansion across the United States and international markets, development of its technology platform, and growth of its engineering and research teams, the company said in a statement.

Meanwhile, the company is launching a data infrastructure network to power the next era of medicine across the US, India, Brazil, and Argentina, with access to over 100 million de-identified patient records.

BioStack creates workflows that bring together clinical information across disparate health systems and geographies. Connecting notes, labs, imaging, medications, treatments and outcomes, the startup strives to provide a comprehensive view of the patient and informs population-level and hospital-level discovery. 

“Collecting every event linked to each patient enables a view of what happens at each stage of a patient's journey.” said Sanat Mishra, Co-founder and CEO of BioStack. “We’re building the infrastructure that connects all of the clinical information and makes it useful, both for clinicians making decisions today and for the researchers and AI developers building the future of medicine.”

The company also creates proprietary datasets from de-identified data that it collects from each provider system. It connects biological and clinical data with treatment histories and long-term outcomes. This helps researchers understand what happened to a patient and how different interventions affected their health over time.

BioStack creates a feedback loop between clinical care and medical innovation. As more longitudinal patient information becomes available, researchers and AI developers can gain a richer understanding of disease progression and treatment response. 

The startup has combined more than several hundred thousand fragmented X-rays, MRIs, and CT scans and over several million telehealth audio transcripts with other pathology and clinical records. The resulting dataset provides a powerful resource for training AI agents to help clinicians evaluate treatment options and likely patient outcomes, said the company.

BioStack currently works with hospitals across the US, Brazil, India and Argentina. This gives the company access to a diverse patient population and healthcare environments.
